transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for calling S-Net technical support, my name is Julian. How can I help you today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hello Julian. I am paying sixty-five pounds a month for your top-tier Fibre 900 package, but every evening between seven PM and ten PM, our download speed collapses down to fifteen megabits! We can't even stream a television show without endless buffering!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I can examine your optical line metrics, Hannah. First I need to complete account verification. What is your full name and the installation address?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hannah Abbott, 19 Woodlands Road, Darlington, DL3 7BF.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And what is the four-digit security PIN on the account?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: So what I understand is you are subscribed to our Fibre 900 tier, but experience severe speed degradation down to fifteen megabits during peak evening hours, impacting streaming and general household browsing, is that right?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, exactly. During the daytime at eleven AM I get nine hundred and twenty megabits, but as soon as peak hours hit, it falls off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: What devices are connected when you measure fifteen megabits?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I tested on my desktop computer wired directly via Cat 6 cable to LAN port 1 of the Hub 5 router.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And is the optical ONT box on the wall showing a solid green PON light during these peak hours?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, the PON light stays solid green, and the LAN light flashes amber with network activity.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That rules out local optical loss of signal. Bear with me for a moment while I query the Darlington exchange aggregation switch telemetry.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for your patience, Hannah. Looking at the GPON optical line terminal statistics for your local splitter, the downstream PON tree is running into severe contention with twenty-eight heavy subscribers on the same optical port.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So you've overloaded the local fibre splitter with too many customers! That is completely unacceptable for a premium package!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Our wholesale provisioning standards allow up to thirty-two endpoints per GPON port, but three commercial accounts on that tree are saturating peak bandwidth.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Well, I shouldn't be penalized with dial-up speeds because of someone else's commercial usage!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Obviously S-Net manages quality of service to ensure residential traffic receives balanced prioritization.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What can be done right now to get my speed back to what I pay for?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I will take direct ownership of this. I have administrative access to the OLT provisioning console, and I can migrate your ONT virtual circuit over to an uncrowded XGS-PON splitter port on card two.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: While we have the diagnostic tool open, what is the optical receive power level showing on the wall unit?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: In the web dashboard, it shows negative eighteen point two dBm.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Negative eighteen dBm is an optimal light level, well within the negative eight to negative twenty-seven tolerance band.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Good to know the physical laser signal from the street is healthy.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And does your computer have a two-point-five gigabit network interface card installed?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, my motherboard has an integrated two-point-five gigabit Intel Ethernet port.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Port 1 on the Hub 5 router supports full two-point-five gigabit auto-negotiation, so there are no local bottleneck points.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That explains why the throughput is so consistently high now.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And we also recommend keeping the router firmware on auto-update to receive optical scheduling patches.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Auto-update is switched on.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And you don't have any third-party VPN software active on that desktop during testing?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No VPNs running, clean native connection.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Can you do that migration remotely without an engineer visit?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes. We can trigger an instantaneous optical port remap from the exchange headend. The ONT will reboot once during the transfer.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Go ahead and run the transfer then. I am tired of paying sixty-five pounds for a premium service that collapses every evening!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Remapping virtual circuit now. Bear with me for sixty seconds while the optical profile re-authenticates.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for holding, Hannah. The ONT has resynchronized onto the dedicated uncrowded XGS-PON port.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The PON light on the wall unit is solid green again.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Just to confirm the test setup before you run a speed test, you are testing on your desktop wired to LAN port 1 with Cat 6, correct?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, wired Cat 6 into port 1.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Please open the S-Net desktop speed test and start a test run.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Starting speed test now... Speed dial is shooting up... Three hundred... Six hundred... Eight hundred and eighty-five megabits download!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And what is the upload speed measuring?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Upload is one hundred and ten megabits with an idle ping of six milliseconds!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That confirms your connection is now running at full gigabit line capacity with zero contention.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That is an astonishing difference. It went from fifteen megabits to nearly nine hundred megabits in ten minutes!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And because that port migration is hardcoded into the OLT routing table, peak evening congestion will no longer affect your line.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That gives me so much peace of mind.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Just to verify your contact billing email on file, it's hannah dot abbott at darlington dot org dot uk, correct?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, that's my email.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I will log the OLT port change in your service history notes for future reference.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you Julian, you knew exactly what buttons to push to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Is there anything else with your Fibre 900 service that I can help with today, Hannah?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, that's everything sorted out completely. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for choosing S-Net, Hannah, and have a wonderful evening.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you Julian, goodbye.
